decks.title: Correlation — Part 1: Meaning, Scatter Diagram and Properties
goals: Define correlation and distinguish positive, negative, linear and non-linear relations
Draw and read a scatter diagram for perfect, high, low and no correlation
Explain why correlation does not prove causation, using a third variable and spurious correlation
State the properties of the coefficient and show that it is unaffected by a change of origin and scale

slides.heading: Correlation
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how two variables **move together**, and how a **scatter diagram** shows it.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: meaning of correlation, scatter diagram, causation caution, properties of the coefficient and the non-linear case
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Do students who study longer score higher marks? Do higher prices mean fewer sales? Correlation is the tool for such questions about two variables. In this part we learn what correlation means, how a scatter diagram shows it, why correlation is not cause, and what properties its coefficient has. All the data are imagined.

slides.heading: What is correlation?
slides.body_md: **Correlation** is the degree and direction of the **linear** relationship between two variables.

rows: The variables rise and fall together
Temperature and cold drink sales at a juice corner
One rises while the other falls
Temperature and hot soup sales at a hill stall
The dots lie around a straight line
Hours of study and marks of a class
Temperature and electricity use in a hill town
Shoe size and marks of students

visual.alt: Table of kinds of correlation, positive, negative, linear, non-linear and none, each with its meaning and an imagined example

slides.narration: Correlation tells us how closely two variables are related along a straight line, and in which direction. If both rise and fall together, the correlation is positive. If one rises while the other falls, it is negative. A relation is linear when the points lie around a straight line, and non linear when they follow a curve.

slides.heading: Drawing a scatter diagram
slides.body_md: Put one variable on each axis and mark a **dot** for every pair of values.
bullets: The dashed lines mark the **means** of the two variables.
Dots in the upper right and lower left sections give positive products of deviations.

slides.heading: Degrees of correlation
slides.body_md: The closer the dots are to a straight line, the **higher** the correlation; the direction gives the **sign**.

rows: All on one rising straight line
All on one falling straight line

visual.caption: Imagined sets of seven dots, as drawn in the figures.

slides.narration: Here are the six cases side by side. Perfect correlation means all the dots lie on one straight line. High correlation means they lie close to a line. Low correlation means they are widely spread. No correlation means no pattern at all. A rising line gives a positive sign and a falling line gives a negative sign.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading a scatter diagram
slides.body_md: An officer of the imagined district of Kaveripur plotted rainfall against paddy yield for seven years. Read the diagram.
bullets: **Direction:** the dots rise from lower left to upper right, so the correlation is positive.
**Closeness:** the dots lie fairly close to a rising line, so it is high.
**Figures:** the mean rainfall is 70 cm and the mean yield is 18 quintals.
**Coefficient:** it works out to **0.86**, a high positive value.

The mean rainfall is 70 centimetres and the mean yield is 18 quintals. The coefficient of correlation is 0.86. Wetter years in this imagined district go with higher yields.

slides.heading: Quick check: does it prove cause?
slides.body_md: A high coefficient between study hours and marks. Does it prove that studying longer causes higher marks?
slides.narration: A coefficient describes how two variables move together. Ask yourself whether anything else could be affecting both of them, such as ability or sleep, before you decide if it proves cause.

slides.heading: Correlation is not causation
slides.body_md: Two variables can move together because a **third variable** affects both.

visual.alt: Flow diagram in which hot sunny weather leads to more ice cream sold and also leads to more sunburn cases, so the two moves together without one causing the other
visual.caption: A third variable moves both

slides.narration: In an imagined seaside town, ice cream sales and sunburn cases rise together. Ice cream does not cause sunburn. Hot sunny weather, a third variable, raises both. So a high coefficient shows that variables move together, but it does not show that one causes the other.

slides.heading: Why a strong correlation may mislead
slides.body_md: A link produced by chance or by a third variable, and not by a real connection, is a **spurious correlation**.

rows: Hot weather raises both ice cream sales and sunburn in a seaside town
Two unrelated series that happen to rise together over a few years
Do firms advertise more because sales are high, or are sales high because of advertising?

visual.alt: Table of three reasons why a strong correlation may not show cause: a third variable, chance and reverse direction, each with an imagined case

slides.narration: There are three common reasons for caution. A third variable may drive both. The link may be pure chance, especially over a few years. Or the direction of influence may be the opposite of what we assume. A link made by chance or a third variable is called a spurious correlation.

slides.heading: Properties of the coefficient
slides.body_md: The coefficient lies between **−1 and +1**, has **no unit**, and ignores a change of **origin** and **scale**.

rows: It is a pure number, because the units of the two variables cancel
Adding or subtracting the same number from every value does not change it
Multiplying or dividing every value by a positive number does not change it
The sign shows direction; the distance from zero shows strength

visual.alt: Table of the properties of the coefficient of correlation: limits, no unit, change of origin, change of scale, and sign and size

slides.narration: The coefficient always lies between negative one and positive one. It has no unit, since the two units cancel out. Adding the same number to every value, or multiplying every value by a positive number, does not change it. Its sign shows the direction and its distance from zero shows the strength.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: origin and scale
slides.body_md: The coefficient for the Lotus Valley data is 0.8. Change the data and see what happens.
bullets: Add 2 to every hours value: the coefficient stays **0.8**.
Divide every mark by 5: it stays **0.8**.
Use u = hours − 6 and v = (marks − 55) ÷ 5: the new values are small, and it is still **0.8**.
Multiply hours by −1: only the sign turns, to **−0.8**.

visual.alt: Table of the coefficient for the imagined Lotus Valley data under changes of origin and scale: original 0.8, hours plus 2 0.8, marks divided by 5 0.8, two transformed versions 0.8 and 0.8, and hours multiplied by negative 1 −0.8
visual.caption: Imagined Lotus Valley School students. Only a negative multiplier reverses the sign.

slides.narration: We changed the imagined Lotus Valley data in several ways. Adding two to the hours leaves the coefficient at 0.8. Dividing the marks by five leaves it at 0.8. A shift of origin together with a change of scale also leaves it at 0.8. Only multiplying one variable by a negative number reverses the sign.

slides.heading: Quick check: a change of origin
slides.body_md: Every student studies 2 hours more, while marks stay the same. What happens to the coefficient?
slides.narration: Adding the same number to every value moves each value and its mean by the same amount. Think about what that does to the deviations from the mean, and so to the coefficient.

slides.heading: When the coefficient is zero
slides.body_md: A coefficient of zero means **no linear** relation. A **curved** relation may still exist.

slides.body_md: Find the coefficient for the imagined hill town of Himgiri.

slides.body_md: Match each pattern of dots with the kind of correlation it shows.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Degree and direction of the linear relationship between two variables
One dot for each pair of values; shows direction and closeness
Perfect: dots on a line, coefficient −1 or +1; none: no pattern, near 0
Correlation does not prove cause; look for a third variable
Between −1 and +1; no unit; unaffected by change of origin and scale
No linear relation, but a curved relation may exist

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: correlation, scatter diagram, perfect and no correlation, causation, properties and the zero coefficient

slides.narration: To recap. Correlation is the degree and direction of the linear relationship between two variables. A scatter diagram shows it with one dot for each pair. Perfect correlation puts all dots on a line. Correlation does not prove cause, because a third variable may be at work. The coefficient lies between negative one and one, has no unit, and ignores a change of origin and scale.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Define correlation as the **degree and direction of the linear relationship**.
Read a scatter diagram for **direction** and **closeness** before naming the degree.
Never say that a high coefficient **proves cause**; name a possible third variable.
State the three properties: **limits, no unit, origin and scale**.
Remember that **zero** means no linear relation, not no relation at all.

Never say that a high coefficient proves cause, and name a possible third variable. State the properties of the coefficient. And remember that zero means no straight line relation, not no relation at all.

decks.title: Correlation — Part 2: Karl Pearson and Spearman
goals: Calculate Karl Pearson's coefficient from deviations and from actual values
Interpret the sign and size of a coefficient
Calculate Spearman's rank correlation, from given ranks and from values
Apply the correction factor for repeated ranks and choose the right measure

slides.heading: Karl Pearson and Spearman
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **measuring** the relationship with a number, from values and from ranks.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: Karl Pearson coefficient, working table, reading the value, rank correlation, ties and the choice of measure
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we turn the picture into a number. First Karl Pearson's coefficient, worked out from deviations, and its actual value form. Then we learn how to read its sign and size. After that comes Spearman's rank correlation, including repeated ranks, and finally a rule for choosing between the two. All data are imagined.

slides.heading: Karl Pearson's coefficient
slides.body_md: With x and y as **deviations from the means**: **r = Σxy ÷ √(Σx² × Σy²)**.

rows: A value of the first variable minus the mean of the first variable
A value of the second variable minus the mean of the second variable
The sum of the products of the paired deviations
The sums of the squared deviations of each variable
Σxy divided by the square root of Σx² times Σy²

visual.alt: Table of the symbols in Karl Pearson's formula: deviations x and y, the sum of products Σxy, the sums of squares Σx² and Σy², and the coefficient r

slides.narration: Karl Pearson's coefficient uses deviations from the means. For each pair we multiply the deviation of the first variable by the deviation of the second, and add these products. We also add the squares of the deviations of each variable. The coefficient is the sum of products divided by the square root of the two sums of squares multiplied together.

slides.heading: Steps of the working
slides.body_md: Work in a table, one column for each quantity, and add each column at the end.

visual.alt: Flow of the steps for Karl Pearson's coefficient: find both means, find deviations, form products and squares, add the columns, then divide the sum of products by the square root of the product of the sums of squares
visual.caption: Steps of the working

slides.narration: The working follows five steps. Find the mean of each variable. Find the deviation of every value from its mean. Form the products of the paired deviations and the squares of each deviation. Add each column. Finally divide the sum of products by the square root of the product of the two sums of squares.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: study hours and marks
slides.body_md: Five imagined students of Lotus Valley School: find the coefficient from the deviations.
bullets: Step 1 — Means: 6 hours and 55 marks.
Step 2 — Totals of the columns: Σxy = 40, Σx² = 10, Σy² = 250.
Step 3 — The root of 10 × 250 is 50.
Step 4 — Divide: **r = 0.8**, a high positive value.

visual.alt: Working table for the imagined Lotus Valley students: Σxy 40, Σx² 10, Σy² 250, coefficient 0.8
visual.caption: Imagined Lotus Valley School students: means 6 and 55.

slides.narration: The deviations of hours from the mean are in the third column and those of marks in the fourth. The products add up to 40, the squares of the hours deviations to 10, and the squares of the marks deviations to 250. The coefficient is 40 divided by 50, which is 0.8.

slides.heading: Quick check: order of the steps
slides.body_md: Put the steps of working out the coefficient in order.
slides.narration: Think about what each step needs. You cannot find deviations before you know the means, and you cannot add the columns before the products and squares are formed. The division comes last.

slides.heading: The actual-value form
slides.body_md: Without deviations: **r = (nΣxy − ΣxΣy) ÷ √[(nΣx² − (Σx)²)(nΣy² − (Σy)²)]**.

rows: Sum of each hours value times its marks value
Sums of squares of the actual values

visual.alt: Table of the actual-value working for the imagined Lotus Valley students: numerator 200, the two parts 50 and 1250, coefficient 0.8, the same as the deviation method
visual.caption: Imagined Lotus Valley School students: the actual-value form gives the same coefficient.

slides.narration: The same coefficient can be found from the actual values, without deviations. We need the number of pairs, the sums of the two variables, the sum of products, and the sums of squares. For the Lotus Valley data the parts are 200, 50 and 1250, and the coefficient is again 0.8. Both forms always agree.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a negative coefficient
slides.body_md: The imagined Mango Mart noted the price of apples and the quantity sold on five days.
bullets: Step 1 — Means: Rs 140 and 40 kg.
Step 2 — Totals: Σxy = −300, Σx² = 1000, Σy² = 250.
Step 3 — The root of 1000 × 250 is 500.
Step 4 — **r = −0.6**: the sign of Σxy decides the sign of r.

visual.alt: Working table for the imagined Mango Mart: Σxy −300, Σx² 1000, Σy² 250, coefficient −0.6
visual.caption: Imagined Mango Mart: means Rs 140 and 40 kg.

slides.narration: Here the products of deviations are mostly negative, so the sum of products is negative 300. The sums of squares are always positive, so the sign of the coefficient is the sign of the sum of products. The coefficient is negative 0.6. On days when the price was higher, the quantity sold tended to be smaller.

slides.narration: Here are the same five days as dots. They fall from upper left to lower right, which is what a negative coefficient looks like. They do not lie exactly on a line, so the relation is moderate, not perfect, and the coefficient of negative 0.6 is a fair summary of it.

slides.heading: Interpreting the size and the sign
slides.body_md: The **sign** gives the direction; the **distance from zero** gives the strength.

visual.alt: Table of values of a coefficient of correlation with a common rough reading: +1 perfect positive, +0.9 very strong positive, +0.3 weak positive, 0 no linear relation, −0.7 fairly strong negative, −1 perfect negative
visual.caption: A rough guide; the bands are not fixed rules. Neither sign nor size proves cause.

slides.narration: A value near one, positive or negative, shows a very strong relation. A value near zero shows a weak one. The sign tells us the direction. So positive point nine is very strong and positive, positive point three is weak and positive, and negative point seven is fairly strong and negative. These bands are only a rough guide, and none of them proves cause.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading a rank correlation
slides.body_md: Two critics' rankings of films give a coefficient of 0.9. What does it mean?
slides.narration: A rank correlation is read just like the other coefficient. Think about how close the value is to one, and what that says about the agreement between the two rankings.

slides.heading: Spearman's rank correlation
slides.body_md: For ranks: **rs = 1 − 6ΣD² ÷ (n³ − n)**, where D is the difference between the two ranks of an item.
bullets: Use it for **qualitative** data that can only be ranked.
Use it when **extreme values** would distort Karl Pearson's coefficient.

nodes.label: Rank each series, 1 for the highest
Tied values share the average rank
Put the total in the formula

visual.alt: Flow of the steps for rank correlation: rank each series from the highest, give tied values the average rank, find the differences and square them, add the correction factor for ties, then use the formula
visual.caption: The rank correlation route

slides.narration: Spearman's rank correlation works with ranks. Rank each series, giving rank one to the highest value. Find the difference between the two ranks of each item and square it. Add the squares and put the total in the formula, which is one minus six times that total divided by n cubed minus n. Use it for qualitative data and for data with extreme values.

slides.heading: Assigning ranks, with ties
slides.body_md: Rank from the **highest** value. Tied values share the places they cover and each gets the **average** rank.

visual.alt: Table of the scores of six imagined players with their ranks 2, 4, 4, 1, 6, 4; the three tied scores share ranks 3 to 5 and each gets 4
visual.caption: Imagined batters: the tied score of 35 takes places 3, 4 and 5, so each gets 4.

slides.narration: Look at the scores of six imagined players. The highest score gets rank one and the next gets rank two. Three players share the same score, and between them they cover places three, four and five. Each gets the average of these, which is 4. The lowest score then takes rank six.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: ranks given by two judges
slides.body_md: Two imagined judges ranked five contestants of a school debate.
bullets: Step 1 — Differences D: 1, 0, -1, -1, 1; they add to 0.
Step 2 — Squares add to ΣD² = **4**.

visual.alt: Working table for two imagined judges of a school debate: the differences 1, 0, -1, -1, 1 add to 0 and the squares add to 4, so the rank correlation is 0.8
visual.caption: Imagined debate contestants. The differences always add to zero.

slides.narration: The differences between the two judges' ranks add up to zero, which is a good check. Their squares add up to 4. With five contestants, n cubed minus n is 120. So the rank correlation is one minus six times 4 divided by 120, which is 0.8. The judges largely agree.

slides.heading: Quick check: a correction factor
slides.body_md: Two students share one score and three others share another. What total correction factor is added?
slides.narration: For each group of tied values the factor is m cubed minus m, divided by twelve, where m is the size of the group. Work out the factor for the group of two, then for the group of three, and add them.

slides.heading: Repeated ranks: the correction factor
slides.body_md: For each group of **m** tied items add **(m³ − m) ÷ 12** to ΣD², then use **rs = 1 − 6(ΣD² + correction) ÷ (n³ − n)**.

visual.alt: Table of the correction factor for groups of 2, 3 and 4 tied items: 0.5, 2, 5
visual.caption: The factor is added to ΣD² once for every tied group.

slides.narration: When values are tied, the rank correlation formula needs a correction. For each group of m tied items we add m cubed minus m, divided by twelve, to the sum of squared differences. A tied pair adds 0.5, a tied group of three adds 2, and a group of four adds five. If there are several groups, add all the factors.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: ranks from values, with a tie
slides.body_md: Six imagined students took a Monday test and a Friday test. Two Monday scores are equal.
bullets: Step 3 — One tied pair: correction factor = **0.5**.

visual.alt: Working table for six imagined students: tied Monday scores share rank 3.5; ΣD² is 6.5, the correction factor is 0.5, and the rank correlation is 0.8
visual.caption: Imagined Sagar Coaching Institute students. One pair of equal Monday scores shares ranks 3 and 4.

slides.narration: The two equal Monday scores cover places three and four, so each gets rank 3.5. The squared differences add up to 6.5, and one tied pair adds a correction of 0.5. The total 7 is put in the formula with six times that total divided by 210. The rank correlation is 0.8.

slides.heading: Pearson or Spearman?
slides.body_md: Choose by the **type of data** and by the presence of **extreme values**.

visual.alt: Table comparing Karl Pearson's coefficient and rank correlation on data, quantities used and extreme values, with the values 0.75 and 1 for the imagined shops
visual.caption: Imagined shops with one very large sales figure.

slides.narration: Use Karl Pearson's coefficient for exactly measured values without extreme ones. Use rank correlation for qualitative data that can only be ranked, and when extreme values are present. For five imagined shops, one with very large sales, Karl Pearson's coefficient is only 0.75, while the rank correlation is 1, since the ranks agree exactly.

sections.heading: 1. Meaning and types of correlation
sections.body_md:
**Correlation** is the degree and direction of the **linear** relationship between two variables. It is **positive** when the variables move in the same direction (both rise and fall together) and **negative** when they move in opposite directions. It is **linear** when the dots of a scatter diagram lie around a straight line and **non-linear** when they follow a curve.

Imagined examples: temperature and cold drink sales at a juice corner (positive); temperature and hot soup sales at a hill stall (negative); shoe size and marks of students (no correlation).

key_terms.definition_md: The degree and direction of the linear relationship between two variables.
A relation in which the variables rise and fall together.
A relation in which one variable rises as the other falls.
A relation in which the paired values lie around a straight line.

rows: The variables rise and fall together
Temperature and cold drink sales at a juice corner

Temperature and hot soup sales at a hill stall
The dots lie around a straight line

sections.heading: 2. Scatter diagram
sections.body_md:
A **scatter diagram** plots one dot for each pair of values, with one variable on each axis. It shows the **direction** of the relation (rising or falling) and its **closeness** (how near the dots lie to a line).

Perfect positive correlation puts all dots on a rising line (coefficient 1); perfect negative on a falling line (−1); high correlation puts the dots close to a line; low correlation spreads them; no correlation shows no pattern (about 0). In the imagined sets of seven dots drawn here the coefficients are 0.86, −0.86, 0.25 and 0.

key_terms.definition_md: A graph with one dot for each pair of values of two variables.
A relation in which all dots lie exactly on one straight line, giving a coefficient of +1 or −1.

sections.heading: 3. Correlation and causation
sections.body_md: A high correlation does **not** prove that one variable **causes** the other. A **third variable** may affect both (in an imagined seaside town, hot weather raises both ice cream sales and sunburn: the coefficient for the imagined five months is 0.96), the link may be **chance**, or the direction of influence may be the reverse. A link caused by chance or by a third variable is a **spurious correlation**.

key_terms.definition_md: A relation in which a change in one variable produces a change in the other.
A correlation between variables that arises from chance or from a common third factor and not from a real connection between them.

sections.heading: 4. Properties of the coefficient
sections.body_md:
1. It lies between **−1 and +1**.
2. It has **no unit**.
3. It is **not affected by a change of origin or scale**: adding the same number to every value, or multiplying or dividing every value by the same positive number, leaves it unchanged. Multiplying one variable by a negative number reverses its sign.
4. A coefficient of **0** shows no **linear** relation; a curved relation may still exist (for the imagined temperature and electricity use of Himgiri the coefficient is 0 although the dots form a U).

For the imagined Lotus Valley data the coefficient is 0.8; after adding 2 to the hours it is 0.8, and after dividing the marks by 5 it is 0.8.

key_terms.definition_md: Adding or subtracting the same number from every value of a variable.
Multiplying or dividing every value of a variable by the same number.
A relation in which the paired values follow a curve and not a straight line.

rows: It is a pure number, because the units of the two variables cancel
Adding or subtracting the same number from every value does not change it
Multiplying or dividing every value by a positive number does not change it
The sign shows direction; the distance from zero shows strength

sections.heading: 5. Karl Pearson's coefficient
sections.body_md:
**r = Σxy ÷ √(Σx² × Σy²)**, where x and y are the deviations of the two series from their means. Work in a table of deviations, products and squares.

For the imagined Lotus Valley students: Σxy = 40, Σx² = 10, Σy² = 250, so r = 40 ÷ 50 = 0.8.

The **actual-value form** is **r = (nΣxy − ΣxΣy) ÷ √[(nΣx² − (Σx)²)(nΣy² − (Σy)²)]**; for the same data it gives 200 ÷ √(50 × 1250) = 0.8. The sign of Σxy is the sign of r.

key_terms.definition_md: A measure of the degree and direction of the linear relationship between two variables, equal to Σxy divided by the square root of Σx² times Σy², with deviations from the means.
The difference between a value and the arithmetic mean of its series.

sections.heading: 6. Spearman's rank correlation
sections.body_md:
**rs = 1 − 6ΣD² ÷ (n³ − n)**, where D is the difference between the two ranks of an item and n is the number of items. Rank 1 is given to the **highest** value. It is used for **qualitative** data that can only be ranked and when **extreme values** are present. The differences D always add up to zero.

**Repeated ranks:** tied values get the average of the ranks they cover, and for each group of m tied items **(m³ − m) ÷ 12** is added to ΣD²: **rs = 1 − 6[ΣD² + Σ(m³ − m) ÷ 12] ÷ (n³ − n)**. Imagined examples: two judges of a debate give rs = 0.8; six students with one tied pair give ΣD² = 6.5, correction 0.5 and rs = 0.8.

sections.body_md:
As a rough guide, a value near +1 shows a very strong positive relation (for example +0.9), a value of about +0.3 a weak positive one, a value near 0 no linear relation, and a value such as −0.7 a fairly strong negative one. These bands are not fixed rules, and no value alone proves cause.

Use **Karl Pearson's coefficient** for exactly measured values and **rank correlation** for ranks, qualitative data and data with extreme values. For five imagined shops, one with very large sales, Karl Pearson's coefficient is 0.75 and rank correlation is 1.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Define correlation as the **degree and direction of the linear relationship** between two variables.
- Read a scatter diagram for **direction and closeness**; never claim that correlation **proves cause**.
- The coefficient lies between **−1 and +1**, has **no unit** and ignores a change of **origin and scale**.

- For rank correlation: rank from the **highest**, check that **ΣD = 0**, add **(m³ − m) ÷ 12** for each tied group.
- Finish every computation with a sentence on **sign and strength**.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best defines correlation between two variables?

options.text_md: It is the average of the two variables
It is the degree and direction of the linear relationship between them
It is the difference between the highest and the lowest value of each variable
It is the cause by which one variable forces the other to change

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It is the degree and direction of the linear relationship between them. Correlation measures how closely, and in which direction, two variables move together in a straight-line pattern. It is not an average of the variables, not a range, and it does not state that one variable causes the other.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Gopal Juice Corner records its daily sales of cold drinks and the afternoon temperature for a month. On hotter days it sells more. The two variables are

options.text_md: negatively correlated, since one rises while the other falls
uncorrelated, since temperature is not controlled by the shop
perfectly correlated, since every hot day has the same sales
positively correlated, since both tend to rise together

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** positively correlated, since both tend to rise together. When higher values of one variable go with higher values of the other, the correlation is positive. Being outside the shop's control does not make them uncorrelated, and the sales need not be identical for the relation to be positive.

questions.stem_md: At the imagined Sundar Soup Stall in a hill town, daily sales of hot soup are noted against the day's temperature. Soup sells more on colder days. The correlation is

options.text_md: negative, since the variables move in opposite directions
positive, since both are recorded daily
zero, since temperature does not depend on the stall
positive, since the stall earns more on busy days

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** negative, since the variables move in opposite directions. As temperature rises, soup sales fall, so the variables move in opposite directions and the correlation is negative. Recording both daily does not make it positive.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined seaside town of Shorepur, monthly sales of ice cream and the number of people swimming at the beach are highly correlated. The most sensible explanation is that

options.text_md: ice cream sales make people swim
swimming makes people buy ice cream and so proves a cause
a third variable, the summer heat, raises both of them
the correlation must be an arithmetic mistake

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a third variable, the summer heat, raises both of them. A third factor, here the heat, can push both variables up together, so a high correlation does not show that either causes the other. The other options claim a cause that the figures cannot show or deny a result that may be correct.

questions.stem_md: A spurious correlation is one in which

options.text_md: two variables have a coefficient of exactly zero
the relationship between the variables is non-linear
two variables appear related, but the link is due to chance or to a third factor rather than a real connection between them
the data come from a sample and not from a census

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** two variables appear related, but the link is due to chance or to a third factor rather than a real connection between them. A spurious correlation looks real in the figures but arises from coincidence or a common third variable. A zero coefficient, a non-linear pattern and sampling are different matters.

questions.stem_md: In a scatter diagram of the daily hours of study and marks of the imagined students of Lotus Valley School, the dots run from the lower left to the upper right. This shows

options.text_md: positive correlation
negative correlation
no correlation
perfect negative correlation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** positive correlation. Dots that rise from lower left to upper right show that large values of one variable go with large values of the other: positive correlation. Falling dots would show negative correlation, and a shapeless cloud no correlation.

questions.stem_md: The dots of a scatter diagram of the shoe sizes and test marks of an imagined Class 11 are spread over the whole graph with no visible direction. The coefficient of correlation is most likely

options.text_md: close to +1
close to −1
greater than +1
close to zero

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** close to zero. A shapeless cloud shows no linear relation, so the coefficient is near zero. A value near +1 or −1 needs dots close to a straight line, and no coefficient can exceed +1.

questions.stem_md: All the dots of a scatter diagram of the price and quantity demanded of an imagined product lie exactly on one falling straight line. The coefficient of correlation is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** −1. Dots on a falling straight line show perfect negative correlation, which is −1. Zero means no linear relation, +1 is a rising line, and −0.5 is a loose falling pattern, not an exact line.

questions.stem_md: A student of the imagined Pinecrest College reports the coefficient of correlation of her data as 1.4. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: It must be wrong, since the coefficient always lies between −1 and +1
It is possible, since it shows a very strong relation
It is possible if the data are in rupees
It is possible only for rank correlation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It must be wrong, since the coefficient always lies between −1 and +1. The coefficient of correlation can never be outside the limits −1 and +1, whatever the units, so 1.4 shows an error in the work. Units and the type of coefficient do not change the limits.

questions.stem_md: The coefficient of correlation between the price of apples in rupees per kg and the quantity sold in kg at the imagined Mango Mart is

options.text_md: measured in rupees per kg
a pure number with no unit
measured in kg
measured in rupees

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a pure number with no unit. The units of the two variables cancel out in the formula, so the coefficient has no unit and can be compared across different studies. It is not in rupees or in kg.

questions.stem_md: The coefficient of correlation between daily hours of study and marks of five imagined students of Lotus Valley School is 0.8. If every student's hours are increased by 2 for a new record, the marks staying the same, the new coefficient is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 0.8. Adding a constant to every value is a change of origin, which leaves the deviations from the mean, and therefore the coefficient, unchanged: 0.8. Adding 2 to the coefficient or doubling it would not follow from the formula, and the relation does not disappear.

questions.stem_md: The marks of the five imagined students of Lotus Valley School are rescaled by dividing each by 5, while hours of study are left as they are. If the original coefficient was 0.8, the coefficient for the rescaled marks is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 0.8. Dividing every value by a positive constant is a change of scale, which does not alter the coefficient: it stays 0.8. Dividing the coefficient by 5, multiplying it by 5, or reversing its sign would not follow, since the dots keep their pattern.

questions.stem_md: The imagined hill town of Himgiri records daily temperature and electricity use: heaters on cold days and fans on hot days make use high at both ends. A coefficient of 0 is found. The correct conclusion is that

options.text_md: temperature and electricity use are unrelated in every way
electricity use is the cause of the temperature
the data must contain an error
there is no linear relation, but a non-linear relation clearly exists

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** there is no linear relation, but a non-linear relation clearly exists. The coefficient measures only linear association. A U-shaped pattern, where use falls and then rises, can give a coefficient of zero although the variables are strongly related. Zero does not prove that no relation of any kind exists.

questions.stem_md: Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation, with x and y as deviations from the respective means, is given by

options.text_md: Σx² divided by the square root of (Σxy × Σy²)
Σxy multiplied by the square root of (Σx² × Σy²)
Σxy divided by the square root of (Σx² × Σy²)
the sum of x divided by the sum of y

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Σxy divided by the square root of (Σx² × Σy²). The coefficient is the sum of the products of deviations divided by the square root of the product of the two sums of squared deviations. The other expressions put the quantities in the wrong places.

questions.stem_md: While working out Karl Pearson's coefficient for an imagined data set, a student finds Σxy to be negative. The coefficient is

options.text_md: positive, since squares are positive
negative, since the denominator is always positive
zero, since the deviations cancel
undefined

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** negative, since the denominator is always positive. The denominator is the square root of a product of sums of squares, which is positive, so the sign of the coefficient is the sign of Σxy. Here it is negative. It is not zero unless Σxy is zero.

questions.stem_md: The Spearman rank correlation coefficient, when no ranks are repeated, is calculated by the formula

options.text_md: 1 − 6ΣD² ÷ (n³ − n)
1 − 6ΣD ÷ (n³ − n)
1 + 6ΣD² ÷ (n³ − n)
1 − 6ΣD² ÷ (n² − n)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 1 − 6ΣD² ÷ (n³ − n). Rank correlation is 1 minus six times the sum of squared rank differences divided by n cubed minus n. Using ΣD (which is always zero), a plus sign, or n squared would give wrong values.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is the best case for using the rank correlation coefficient?

options.text_md: Two exactly measured series of rainfall and yield with no unusual values
Two judges ranking contestants of an imagined talent show on stage presence, which cannot be measured in numbers
Two series that each contain several thousand observations
Two series that are perfectly linear

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Two judges ranking contestants of an imagined talent show on stage presence, which cannot be measured in numbers. Rank correlation suits qualitative characteristics that can be ranked but not measured, and also data with extreme values. Exactly measured, well-behaved series are handled by Karl Pearson's coefficient.

questions.stem_md: Four imagined contestants score 90, 70, 70 and 60 and are ranked from the highest. The two who score 70 would occupy the second and third places together, so each is given the rank
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 2.5. Tied values share the ranks they would have taken and each gets the average of these ranks: (2 + 3) ÷ 2 = 2.5. Giving both rank 2 or both rank 3 would favour or penalise them, and 1.5 is wrongly placed.

questions.stem_md: In ranking the monthly sales of an imagined set of shops, three shops are found to have the same sales. The correction factor to be added to ΣD² for this group of three is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 2. For a group of m tied items the factor is (m³ − m) ÷ 12. With m = 3 it is (27 − 3) ÷ 12 = 2. 0.5 is the factor for a pair, and 3 and 27 are parts of the formula, not its value.

questions.stem_md: A rank correlation coefficient of 0.9 between the rankings of two imagined critics of a film festival means that

options.text_md: the critics disagree almost completely
ninety per cent of the films were ranked equally
the critics' rankings agree closely
the critics ranked the films in exactly opposite order

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the critics' rankings agree closely. A coefficient near +1 shows strong agreement between the two rankings. It does not mean that 90 per cent of films have the same rank, and opposite orders would give a value near −1.

questions.stem_md: The coefficient of correlation between the number of hours of television watched and the marks of imagined Class 11 students of Riverdale School is −0.7. The best reading is

options.text_md: watching television lowers marks by exactly 70 per cent
there is a weak relation between the variables
students who watch more television tend to score fewer marks, with a fairly strong relation, though this alone does not prove cause
watching more television raises marks

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** students who watch more television tend to score fewer marks, with a fairly strong relation, though this alone does not prove cause. A value of −0.7 is a fairly strong negative association: the variables tend to move in opposite directions. It says nothing about a 70 per cent effect, it is not weak, and a rise in marks would need a positive sign.

questions.stem_md: In working out the rank correlation of two sets of ranks, a student finds that the differences D between the ranks add up to 2. This shows that

options.text_md: there is an error, since the sum of the rank differences must be zero
the coefficient is 2
the coefficient is negative
the two sets have tied ranks

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** there is an error, since the sum of the rank differences must be zero. Both sets of ranks have the same total, so the differences between them always add to zero. A different total signals a slip. It does not give the coefficient or its sign.

questions.stem_md: Monthly sales (Rs thousand) of five imagined shops are 20, 24, 28, 32, 200 and their customer ratings are 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. One shop has a very large sales figure. Compared with the rank correlation, Karl Pearson's coefficient for these data is

options.text_md: 1, the same as the rank correlation
0.75, higher than the rank correlation
0.75, with a changed sign
0.75, lower than the rank correlation of 1, because the extreme value pulls it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 0.75, lower than the rank correlation of 1, because the extreme value pulls it. The ratings rise with sales at every step, so the rankings agree exactly and the rank coefficient is 1. The very large sales figure stretches the scale and brings Karl Pearson's coefficient down to 0.75. Rank correlation is therefore preferred when extreme values are present.

questions.stem_md: Six imagined contestants of a quiz in the Sunrise Club are ranked by two judges. The value of n³ − n in the denominator of the rank correlation formula is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 210. With n = 6, n³ − n = 216 − 6 = 210. 216 forgets to subtract n, 30 uses n squared, and 36 is not part of the formula.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A high correlation between two variables does not prove that one of them causes the other.

**Reason (R):** A third variable may affect both of them, or the link may be chance.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A. If a common factor or chance can produce the pattern, a high coefficient alone cannot establish cause.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The coefficient of correlation lies between −1 and +1.

**Reason (R):** Rank correlation is used when the characteristics can only be ranked.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. The limits come from the way the coefficient is built from deviations, whereas R states when rank correlation is applied.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Subtracting the same number from every value of a variable does not change the coefficient of correlation.

**Reason (R):** The coefficient is worked out from deviations from the means, and these deviations stay the same after the subtraction.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A. A change of origin shifts each value and its mean by the same amount, so every deviation is unchanged.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** If the coefficient of correlation of two variables is zero, there is no relationship of any kind between them.

**Reason (R):** The coefficient of correlation measures only the linear relationship between two variables.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: a curved, for example U-shaped, relation can give zero. R is true, and it is the reason why a zero value shows only the absence of a linear relation.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When two values of a series are equal, each is given the average of the ranks they would otherwise occupy.

**Reason (R):** When ranks are repeated, the rank correlation formula cannot be used at all.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: the formula is still used, with a correction factor of (m³ − m) ÷ 12 added to ΣD² for each group of m repeated ranks.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Because the coefficient for hours of study and marks of the imagined students of Lotus Valley School is 0.8, studying longer must be the cause of the higher marks.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** A high coefficient shows association, not cause. Other factors, such as ability or sleep, may affect both.

questions.stem_md: True or false? For the debate ranks given by two judges, 3, 1, 4, 2, 5 and 2, 1, 5, 3, 4, the differences of the ranks add up to 0.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The differences are 1, 0, -1, -1, 1, which add up to 0, as they must for two sets of ranks of the same items.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A coefficient of correlation of +0.5 shows a stronger relationship than a coefficient of −0.8, because it is positive.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Strength depends on the distance from zero, not on the sign. −0.8 is farther from zero than +0.5, so it shows the stronger relationship; the sign shows only the direction.

questions.stem_md: In Karl Pearson's formula, x and y stand for the deviations of the observations from their respective ___.
questions.solution_md: The deviations are measured from the arithmetic means of the two series.

questions.stem_md: When ranks are repeated, the term added to ΣD² for each group of m tied items is called the ___ factor.
questions.solution_md: It is the correction factor, (m³ − m) ÷ 12.

questions.stem_md: Match each value of a coefficient of correlation with its usual reading.
questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). A value of +1 is perfect positive; a value near −0.9 is a high negative relation; a value near 0.25 is low and positive; and 0 shows no linear relation.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Lotus Valley School noted the daily hours of study (x) and the marks (y) of five students: 4 hours and 50 marks; 5 hours and 45 marks; 6 hours and 55 marks; 7 hours and 65 marks; 8 hours and 60 marks. Find Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation, correct to two decimals.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Means are 6 hours and 55 marks.
Step 2: Deviations x are -2, -1, 0, 1, 2; deviations y are -5, -10, 0, 10, 5.
Step 3: Σxy = 40, Σx² = 10, Σy² = 250.
Step 4: r = 40 ÷ √(10 × 250) = 40 ÷ 50 = 0.8.

questions.stem_md: At the imagined Mango Mart the price of apples (Rs per kg) and the quantity sold (kg a day) on five days were: Rs 120 and 50 kg; Rs 130 and 35 kg; Rs 140 and 40 kg; Rs 150 and 45 kg; Rs 160 and 30 kg. Find the coefficient of correlation between price and quantity.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Means are Rs 140 and 40 kg.
Step 2: Deviations x are -20, -10, 0, 10, 20; deviations y are 10, -5, 0, 5, -10.
Step 3: Σxy = -300, Σx² = 1000, Σy² = 250.
Step 4: r = -300 ÷ √(1000 × 250) = -300 ÷ 500 = -0.6.

questions.stem_md: For seven years in the imagined district of Kaveripur, rainfall (cm) and paddy yield (quintals per hectare) were: 40 and 12; 50 and 14; 60 and 18; 70 and 16; 80 and 22; 90 and 24; 100 and 20. Find the coefficient of correlation, correct to two decimals.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Means are 70 cm and 18 quintals.
Step 2: Σxy = 480, Σx² = 2800, Σy² = 112.
Step 3: r = 480 ÷ √(2800 × 112) = 480 ÷ 560 = 0.86.

questions.stem_md: For the paddy and rainfall figures of the imagined village of Kedarpur, the deviations from the means gave Σxy = 96, Σx² = 100 and Σy² = 144. Find the coefficient of correlation.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Σx² × Σy² = 100 × 144 = 14400; its square root is 120.
Step 2: r = 96 ÷ 120 = 0.8.

questions.stem_md: For the five students of the imagined Lotus Valley School the coefficient between hours of study x and marks y is 0.8. A teacher defines u = x − 6 and v = (y − 55) ÷ 5 for each student. Find the coefficient of correlation between u and v.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Subtracting 6 and 55 is a change of origin, and dividing by 5 is a change of scale. Neither alters the coefficient.
Step 2: Check with the new values: u = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, v = -1, -2, 0, 2, 1, Σuv = 8, Σu² = 10, Σv² = 10, so the coefficient is 8 ÷ 10 = 0.8.

questions.stem_md: Daily temperature (degrees) and electricity use (units) in the imagined hill town of Himgiri over seven days: 12 and 26; 16 and 16; 20 and 10; 24 and 8; 28 and 10; 32 and 16; 36 and 26. Find the coefficient of correlation.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Means are 24 degrees and 16 units.
Step 2: Deviations x are -12, -8, -4, 0, 4, 8, 12; deviations y are 10, 0, -6, -8, -6, 0, 10.
Step 3: The products of the deviations are -120, 0, 24, 0, -24, 0, 120, so Σxy = 0.
Step 4: r = 0 ÷ √(448 × 336) = 0, although use is closely tied to temperature in a curve.

questions.stem_md: The actual-value form of Karl Pearson's coefficient has the numerator n Σxy − Σx Σy. For the five imagined students of Lotus Valley School (hours 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; marks 50, 45, 55, 65, 60), Σx = 30, Σy = 275 and Σxy = 1690. Find the value of the numerator.

Two imagined judges ranked five contestants (Meera, Karan, Tara, Imran, Nisha) of a school debate. The first judge's ranks are 3, 1, 4, 2, 5 and the second judge's ranks are 2, 1, 5, 3, 4. Find the rank correlation coefficient.

Six imagined kiosks near a bus stand have distances from the stand (hundred metres) of 12, 3, 18, 9, 15, 6 and daily sales (Rs) of 390, 690, 590, 510, 450, 640. Rank each series from the highest value and find the rank correlation coefficient.

questions.stem_md: Six imagined students of the Sagar Coaching Institute scored 72, 65, 65, 80, 58, 50 in a Monday test and 74, 64, 57, 80, 70, 40 in a Friday test. Rank both series from the highest score, treating repeated scores as tied, and find the rank correlation coefficient.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Ranks in the Monday test: 2, 3.5, 3.5, 1, 5, 6; in the Friday test: 2, 4, 5, 1, 3, 6.
Step 2: D = 0, -0.5, -1.5, 0, 2, 0; ΣD² = 6.5.
Step 3: One group of 2 tied, so the correction factor is 0.5.
Step 4: rs = 1 − 6 × (6.5 + 0.5) ÷ 210 = 1 − 0.2 = 0.8.

questions.stem_md: At the imagined Sundarpur fair, seven stalls had visitors (hundreds) of 85, 70, 70, 64, 58, 52, 45 and sales (Rs thousand) of 92, 88, 80, 40, 60, 60, 55. Rank each series from the highest value, using average ranks for ties, and find the rank correlation coefficient.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Ranks of visitors: 1, 2.5, 2.5, 4, 5, 6, 7; ranks of sales: 1, 2, 3, 7, 4.5, 4.5, 6.
Step 2: D = 0, 0.5, -0.5, -3, 0.5, 1.5, 1; ΣD² = 13.
Step 3: Each series has one tied pair, so the correction factor is 1.
Step 4: rs = 1 − 6 × (13 + 1) ÷ 336 = 0.75.

questions.stem_md: Eight imagined trainees at the Orion Training Hub scored 90, 80, 75, 75, 75, 60, 55, 40 in theory and 96, 91, 84, 50, 41, 70, 58, 64 in practical. Rank both series from the highest, with average ranks for ties, and find the rank correlation coefficient.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Theory ranks: 1, 2, 4, 4, 4, 6, 7, 8; practical ranks: 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 4, 6, 5.
Step 2: D = 0, 0, 1, -3, -4, 2, 1, 3; ΣD² = 40.
Step 3: Three trainees tie, so the correction factor is (27 − 3) ÷ 12 = 2.
Step 4: rs = 1 − 6 × (40 + 2) ÷ 504 = 1 − 0.5 = 0.5.

questions.stem_md: Five imagined shops had monthly sales (Rs thousand) of 20, 24, 28, 32, 200 and customer ratings of 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. Find the rank correlation coefficient between sales and ratings.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Ranks of sales: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1; ranks of ratings: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1.
Step 2: The ranks are identical, so every D is 0 and ΣD² = 0.
Step 3: rs = 1 − 0 = 1, even though the extreme value of 200 gives Karl Pearson's coefficient only 0.75.

questions.stem_md: Define correlation and state what its sign shows.
questions.solution_md: Definition and meaning of the sign.

answer.model_answer_md: **Correlation** measures how closely two variables are related along a straight line, and in which direction. A **positive** sign shows that the variables move in the same direction, and a **negative** sign shows that they move in opposite directions.

marking_scheme.step: Meaning of positive and negative sign

questions.stem_md: Give one imagined example each of positive and of negative correlation between two variables of a village market.
questions.solution_md: One example of each kind, with the direction explained.

answer.model_answer_md: **Positive:** the number of customers at an imagined village market and its daily sales, since both rise together. **Negative:** the price of tomatoes and the quantity bought, since buyers purchase less when the price is higher.

questions.stem_md: A scatter diagram of the shoe sizes and the marks of the imagined students of Green Hill College shows dots spread all over the graph. What does it show, and what is the likely value of the coefficient?
questions.solution_md: No correlation, coefficient near zero.

answer.model_answer_md: The dots show **no correlation**: shoe size gives no guidance about marks. The coefficient of correlation is likely to be **close to zero**, as there is no straight-line pattern.

questions.stem_md: Between which limits does the coefficient of correlation lie? What do the two limits show?
questions.solution_md: Limits −1 and +1, and their meaning.

answer.model_answer_md: The coefficient lies between **−1 and +1**. The value **+1** shows perfect positive correlation, with all dots on a rising straight line, and **−1** shows perfect negative correlation, with all dots on a falling straight line.

questions.stem_md: The coefficient between hours of study and marks of the imagined students is 0.8. What is the coefficient if every mark is multiplied by 2 and then increased by 10? Give a reason.
questions.solution_md: The coefficient stays 0.8.

answer.model_answer_md: The coefficient stays **0.8**. Multiplying by a positive number is a change of scale and adding 10 is a change of origin; the coefficient is not affected by either, because it is a ratio built from deviations from the means.

questions.stem_md: A report on an imagined town notes that the number of fire engines sent to a fire and the damage done are positively correlated, and concludes that fire engines cause damage. Why is this conclusion not justified?
questions.solution_md: Third variable, the size of the fire.

answer.model_answer_md: Correlation does not prove **causation**. A **third variable**, the size of the fire, raises both the number of engines sent and the damage done, so the link is not one of cause and effect.

questions.stem_md: Six imagined batters scored 48, 35, 35, 62, 20, 35 runs in a match. Rank them from the highest score, giving tied scores the average rank.

answer.model_answer_md: The ranks are **2, 4, 4, 1, 6, 4**. The highest score, 62, has rank 1 and 48 has rank 2. The three batters on 35 would occupy ranks 3, 4 and 5, so each gets (3 + 4 + 5) ÷ 3 = **4**. The score 20 is last, with rank 6.

marking_scheme.step: Average rank of the tied scores

questions.stem_md: In ranking an imagined series, one group of two values and one group of three values are tied. State the correction factor for each group and its total.
questions.solution_md: Factors 0.5 and 2; total 2.5.

answer.model_answer_md: For a group of m tied items the factor is (m³ − m) ÷ 12. For the pair it is (8 − 2) ÷ 12 = **0.5**; for the group of three it is (27 − 3) ÷ 12 = **2**. The total to be added to ΣD² is **2.5**.

marking_scheme.step: Formula applied to the two groups

questions.stem_md: State two situations in which the rank correlation coefficient is preferred to Karl Pearson's coefficient.
questions.solution_md: Qualitative characteristics; extreme values.

answer.model_answer_md: Rank correlation is preferred when the characteristics are **qualitative**, such as honesty or beauty, and can only be ranked, and when the data contain **extreme values** that would distort Karl Pearson's coefficient.

questions.stem_md: Interpret coefficients of +0.9, +0.3 and −0.7 between the monthly spending on advertisements and sales of imagined firms.
questions.solution_md: Strong positive, weak positive, fairly strong negative.

answer.model_answer_md: A value of **+0.9** shows a very strong positive relation; **+0.3** shows a weak positive relation; **−0.7** shows a fairly strong negative relation, in which higher advertising goes with lower sales. None of them alone proves cause.

questions.stem_md: State any three properties of the coefficient of correlation.
questions.solution_md: Three properties.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It lies between **−1 and +1**.
2. It has **no unit**: the units of the two variables cancel in the ratio.
3. It is **not affected by a change of origin or scale**, so adding the same number to every value, or multiplying every value by a positive number, leaves it unchanged.

questions.stem_md: For seven days in the imagined hill town of Himgiri, temperature in degrees was 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36 and electricity use in units was 26, 16, 10, 8, 10, 16, 26. The coefficient is 0. Explain why this does not mean that the variables are unrelated.
questions.solution_md: Σxy = 0, so r = 0; the relation is U-shaped, not linear.

answer.model_answer_md: Use is highest at both the lowest and the highest temperatures and lowest in the middle, a **U-shaped** pattern. The deviations from the means give Σxy = **0**, because the positive and negative products cancel. The coefficient measures only the **linear** relation, so 0 shows that there is no linear relation, while a strong **non-linear** relation exists.

questions.stem_md: For the imagined Haven Cafe the deviation totals are Σxy = −72, Σx² = 64 and Σy² = 225. Find Karl Pearson's coefficient and interpret it.
questions.solution_md: r = −0.6, a moderate negative relation.

answer.model_answer_md: Karl Pearson's coefficient is r = Σxy ÷ √(Σx² × Σy²) = −72 ÷ √(64 × 225) = −72 ÷ 120 = **−0.6**. The sign is negative, so the weekly rent and the number of customers move in opposite directions, and a size of 0.6 shows a moderate relation, neither very weak nor very strong.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined art teachers ranked five paintings. The first gave ranks 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and the second gave 3, 1, 2, 5, 4 to the same paintings in the same order. Find the rank correlation coefficient.

answer.model_answer_md: The rank differences are D = -2, 1, 1, -1, 1, which add up to 0 as they should. Their squares add up to ΣD² = **8**. With n = 5, n³ − n = 125 − 5 = 120. Then rs = 1 − 6 × 8 ÷ 120 = 1 − 0.4 = **0.6**, a fairly strong agreement between the two teachers.

questions.stem_md: Compare Karl Pearson's coefficient with the rank correlation coefficient on the type of data, the effect of extreme values and the quantities used.
questions.solution_md: Three points of comparison.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Type of data.** Pearson's coefficient needs measured values; rank correlation can be used for ranks and qualitative data.
2. **Extreme values.** Pearson's coefficient is affected by them; rank correlation is much less affected, since only ranks are used.
3. **Quantities used.** Pearson uses deviations from the means; rank correlation uses differences of ranks.

questions.stem_md: Which coefficient would you choose in (i) the grades given by two imagined teachers to the neatness of the notebooks of ten pupils, and (ii) the weights and heights of the same ten pupils? Give a reason for each.
questions.solution_md: Rank correlation for neatness; Pearson for weight and height.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Rank correlation**: neatness cannot be measured exactly, only ranked, so the grades are turned into ranks.
(ii) **Karl Pearson's coefficient**: weights and heights are measured exactly, so deviations from the means can be used, unless an extreme value is present.

questions.stem_md: Describe how a scatter diagram of two variables is drawn, and explain what it shows in the cases of perfect positive, perfect negative, high, low and no correlation.
questions.solution_md: Drawing, and the five patterns.

answer.model_answer_md: Mark one variable on the horizontal axis and the other on the vertical axis, and put a **dot** for each pair of values. If all dots lie on a **rising** straight line, correlation is **perfect positive**; on a **falling** line, **perfect negative**. Dots close to a line show **high** correlation, dots widely spread around a trend show **low** correlation, and a shapeless cloud shows **no** correlation.

questions.stem_md: The coefficient between daily hours of study (x) and marks (y) of the five imagined students of Lotus Valley School is 0.8. Show, using u = x − 6 and v = (y − 55) ÷ 5, that the coefficient is not affected by a change of origin and scale, and state two other properties.
questions.solution_md: New coefficient 0.8, equal to the original 0.8.

answer.model_answer_md: Subtracting 6 from the hours and 55 from the marks, and dividing the marks by 5, gives u = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 and v = -1, -2, 0, 2, 1. Their means are zero, so the deviations are these values themselves. Then Σuv = 8, Σu² = 10 and Σv² = 10, so the coefficient is 8 ÷ √(10 × 10) = 8 ÷ 10 = **0.8**, the same as the original 0.8. Two other properties: the coefficient lies between **−1 and +1**, and it has **no unit**.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Anjali Tuition Centre charged monthly fees (Rs hundred) of 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 over five terms, when the enrolments (in tens) were 8, 6, 9, 4, 3. Calculate Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation and interpret it.

answer.model_answer_md: The means are fee 7 and enrolment 6. The deviations of the fee are -4, -2, 0, 2, 4 and those of the enrolment are 2, 0, 3, -2, -3. The products of the deviations add up to Σxy = **-24**, and the squares give Σx² = **40** and Σy² = **26**. So r = −24 ÷ √(40 × 26) = −24 ÷ 32.25 = **−0.74**. This is a fairly strong negative correlation: higher fees go with fewer students enrolled.

questions.stem_md: Six imagined students of the Sagar Coaching Institute scored 72, 65, 65, 80, 58, 50 in a Monday test and 74, 64, 57, 80, 70, 40 in a Friday test. Find the rank correlation coefficient, using a correction for the tied scores, and interpret it.

answer.model_answer_md: Ranking from the highest, the Monday scores take ranks 2, 3.5, 3.5, 1, 5, 6 and the Friday scores take ranks 2, 4, 5, 1, 3, 6, the equal Monday scores sharing the average rank 3.5. The differences are 0, -0.5, -1.5, 0, 2, 0, so ΣD² = **6.5**. One pair is tied, so the correction factor is (8 − 2) ÷ 12 = **0.5**. Then rs = 1 − 6 × (6.5 + 0.5) ÷ 210 = 1 − 0.2 = **0.8**: a strong agreement between the two tests.

marking_scheme.step: Ranks with average rank for the tie

questions.stem_md: Monthly sales (Rs thousand) of five imagined shops were 20, 24, 28, 32, 200 with customer ratings of 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. Find the rank correlation, state Karl Pearson's coefficient (0.75) and explain which is better and why.
questions.solution_md: rs = 1 against r = 0.75.

answer.model_answer_md: The sales rank as 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 and the ratings rank as 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. The two sets of ranks agree exactly, so every difference is zero, ΣD² = 0 and rs = 1 − 0 = **1**. Karl Pearson's coefficient is only **0.75**, because the very large sales figure of 200 thousand stretches the scale and dominates the deviations. Rank correlation is the better measure here: it uses only the order of the values, so it is little affected by an extreme value, and it shows that the ratings rise with sales at every step.

marking_scheme.step: Effect of the extreme value explained

questions.stem_md: A report on the imagined town of Seaview finds that ice cream sales and the number of sunburn cases move together closely. Explain why this does not show that ice cream causes sunburn. Use the ideas of causation, a third variable and spurious correlation.
questions.solution_md: Causation, third variable and spurious correlation.

answer.model_answer_md: A high coefficient shows only that two variables move together; it does not prove that one **causes** the other. Here the **third variable**, hot sunny weather, raises both ice cream sales and sunburn. A link produced in this way, or by chance, is called a **spurious correlation**. To claim cause one needs a clear mechanism and evidence that other factors have been ruled out.
